summary:
El Callao, the department containing Peru's principal international gateway, stands under the national framework. No department-specific trans law, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding appears in the sources, so what a trans visitor faces in El Callao is what Peru's national rules deliver. Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but its Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

The governing instrument is the April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents. Its Article 5.1 prohibits any person from entering or using a public sanitary facility designated for a sex other than their birth sex, with narrow exceptions for custody and for cases where required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities. The same package obliges venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs and bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. A visitor who is visibly trans should expect to be refused entry to gendered facilities across the country, including at airports, hotels, shopping centres and public buildings.

The provision was fast-tracked. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Comisión de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, which still required plenary backing. On 2 April 2025 the plenary approved the dictamen and waived a second vote. The reported trigger was a July 2023 complaint about gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez international airport, the country's main port of entry for international visitors.

The Inter-American human-rights framework points the other way. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru reads Article 5.1 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors.

Enforcement reaches private life as well as public facilities. Consumer-protection body INDECOPI dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit in Resolution 0735-2022, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the national identity card. Activist and journalist Gianna Camacho argues that enforcement of the 2025 ban would rest on security staff checking the identity card to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender. Gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive, so many trans people, including visitors, cannot obtain documents matching their presentation.

Hostility has been voiced from national platforms. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'. A congressman, Lizarzaburu, made dehumanising comparisons on the floor of Congress, as recorded by IDEHPUCP.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia recorded 54 killings of LGBT people and 170 rights-violation cases between 2020 and 2023; the homicide victims were 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian. Nineteen killings occurred in 2023 alone, twelve of them trans women, and perpetrators were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, including 13 of the 19 in 2023. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

Named cases illustrate the risk. In February 2023 the trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano, 31, was kidnapped from central Lima by the 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots. Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot days earlier; two killers were arrested in March 2023. Trans women engaged in sex work face elevated exposure to organised extortion and lethal violence.

Legal recourse is slow but not absent. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reached through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Hate-crime coverage is absent. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. Peru is now one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law. The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
tangentialFactors:
The bathroom restriction is a national measure with a sub-national origin point: the July 2023 complaint about restroom labelling at Jorge Chávez international airport, which sits at the department's core. Visitors arriving by air encounter the policy's political origin at the moment of landing, though the sources record no enforcement incident at the airport itself.

Peru's isolation on hate-crime law is regional. With Paraguay and Guyana it is one of only three South American states without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime provisions, while the Inter-American Court's Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 binds the opposite direction and produced the region's first torture-by-discrimination judgment in the Azul Rojas Marín case.

The gap between law and record is acknowledged by those who keep it. Gianna Camacho, co-author of the 2024 hate-crime findings, states that official counts are a sub-registry; the state has not integrated sexual orientation or gender identity into crime-registration systems, and perpetrators went unidentified in nearly half the 54 homicides recorded for 2020 to 2023.

The 2025 law's speech provisions extend beyond facilities. Human Rights Watch characterises the child-protection framing as a vehicle for repression and the scapegoating of trans people, and the obscenity minimum rose from three to four years, raising the cost of public visibility for trans performers, educators and community organisers.
localsOnly:
Gender-identity recognition in Peru is long, costly and invasive, so a substantial share of trans residents live with identity documents that do not match their presentation. SmartFit grounded restroom assignment on the sex recorded in the national identity card, and INDECOPI dismissed the resulting complaint in Resolution 0735-2022, indicating that document-based exclusion is unlikely to be remedied through the consumer-protection route.

Healthcare settings changed direction in June 2024, when health authorities removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official guidance. Residents navigating clinics and hospitals in El Callao work under that revised national standard, though the sources do not record implementation data at department level.

Community organisers face the article 4 media and advertising content ban and a raised obscenity minimum, both of which bear on local events, publishing, signage and public education. Venue operators in the department are separately obliged by the 2025 package not to post ambiguous restroom signs.
outOfScopeNotes:
No El Callao-specific provision, ordinance, incident or enforcement finding appears in the sources. The department is scored against the national framework, and the only geographically adjacent item, the July 2023 airport restroom complaint, is reported as a trigger for national legislation rather than as a departmental enforcement event.

Whether the April 2025 facility ban has produced prosecutions, fines or security-guard interventions at points of entry in El Callao is unresolved; the sources record the constitutional text, the legislative route and one pre-existing consumer-protection decision, but no post-April 2025 enforcement case.

The geographic distribution of the 54 killings and 170 rights-violation cases recorded for 2020 to 2023 is not broken down by department in the material available, so the share attributable to El Callao cannot be stated. The 26 homicides with unidentified perpetrators, including 13 of the 19 in 2023, further limit any local attribution.

The implementation status of the July 2025 Lima constitutional court ruling against an anti-equality decree, and whether it has any bearing on the April 2025 facility provision, is not resolved in the sources.
